reference_method: Use the unslashed problem text in 英語長文基本.pdf together with the corresponding slash-reading presentation in 英語長文基本解答.pdf. The answer book is authoritative for slash placement and Japanese chunk correspondence. Preserve the reference's relatively fine front-to-back chunking; do not replace it with generic grammar heuristics.

rules.rule: Use relatively fine meaning chunks so a learner can process the English from left to right. Long sentences should normally contain multiple slashes when the reference would separate meaningful units. Do not leave most longer sentences unsplit.
Time, place, duration and other readable adjuncts are often separate chunks.
examples: I visited America / last year / and stayed there / for two months.
I read books / at home / on Saturday, / and I went to see a movie, Love with Me, / on Sunday.
We practice / from Monday / to Saturday.

rules.rule: Purpose infinitives are commonly separated from the preceding core clause.
examples: I went to school / to study English.
I'm going to the playground / to practice soccer.
My sister is coming / to see me.

rules.rule: Because, if, when and similar subordinate clauses are separated when they form a clear reading unit, including clause-first structures.
examples: I'm glad to meet you / because you can speak English very well.
If you are interested, / you should go / on a weekday.
Well, / after you watch the game today, / if you like our team, / you can join us.

rules.rule: Coordinated clauses and major coordinated units are frequently separated. Conjunctions/discourse connectives may remain with the next unit or stand as a short chunk when the reference does so.
examples: The movie is very popular, / so a lot of people go to see it / on the weekend.
It will start / at four, / and we will play / at our playground.
So, / I think, / about five or six days a week, / after school.

rules.rule: Prepositional phrases and passive-agent phrases may be separated as their own reading chunks. Do not impose a generic ban on splitting a predicate before a following prepositional phrase.
examples: I went to see it / with my friends.
The book was written / by a famous writer.
We saw many kinds of animals / from all over the world.

rules.rule: Verbs of knowing/thinking can be followed by a separate content-clause chunk when the reference does so.
examples: I didn't know / that there is a soccer team / in this school.
I think / I'm good at playing soccer / because I practiced hard.

rules.rule: Short discourse markers, greetings and response units are frequently isolated when they help left-to-right processing.
examples: Yes, / can I help you?
Also, / I'm in the English club / in this school.
Well, / I stayed at home / on Saturday / because it was raining.
Sure. / I'll talk to my team / about it.

rules.rule: Questions may be split before time/place adjuncts and vocatives, rather than being kept as one whole sentence.
examples: What did you do / last Sunday, / Kenta?
What did you do / on the weekend, / Tina?
How about going there / next Sunday?

rules.rule: The reference sometimes separates a long subject or predicate/complement sequence for reading support. Therefore generic rules such as 'never split be + complement' are not authoritative.
examples: Playing in bad weather / isn't difficult / for me.

rules.rule: Do not mechanically force a slash into every short/simple sentence. Some complete short sentences remain unsplit in the reference when no extra reading chunk is useful.
examples: You speak English very well.
The other team is from the school in the next town.
Have you ever played soccer?

rules.rule: Within one dialogue turn, slashes can separate complete neighboring sentences as well as sentence-internal chunks.
examples: I'm his brother. / My name is Paul. / Nice to meet you.
It was very exciting. / I went to see it / with my friends. / They liked it, too.

rules.rule: The Japanese reading-support line must correspond chunk-for-chunk in the same left-to-right order. It is a front-to-back support gloss, not merely an unrelated natural full translation placed underneath.
Slash placement is determined from the reference's reading units, not a fixed word-count interval. Density should resemble the supplied answer-book examples across HOP/STEP/JUMP levels.

benchmark_examples.english: Thank you. / I visited America / last year / and stayed there / for two months.
I went to school / to study English. / Also, / I'm in the English club / in this school.
What did you do / last Sunday, / Kenta?
If you are interested, / you should go / on a weekday. / The movie is very popular, / so a lot of people go to see it / on the weekend.
benchmark_examples.purpose: if clause + main clause + time + result coordination + time
